ARLA Propertymark

items.html: Propertymark is the professional body for the property sector; ARLA is its lettings arm. A Propertymark Protected agent must meet entry requirements, hold Client Money Protection and professional indemnity insurance, keep client money in a separate designated account, submit to an annual accountant’s report, and follow the Propertymark Conduct and Membership Rules.
items.text: Propertymark is the professional body for the property sector; ARLA is its lettings arm. A Propertymark Protected agent must meet entry requirements, hold Client Money Protection and professional indemnity insurance, keep client money in a separate designated account, submit to an annual accountant's report, and follow the Propertymark Conduct and Membership Rules.

items.html: Client Money Protection is the part that matters most, and it is worth being precise about it. It is a government-approved guarantee that stands behind client money itself: rent, deposits held by the agent, repair floats and service charge funds are all covered by the scheme, independently of any one agency. It has been a legal requirement for every letting agent in England since 2019, but the client account behind it is only inspected annually by an independent accountant if the agent belongs to a body like Propertymark. We do.

Deposit Protection Service

items.html: Every deposit taken on an assured tenancy must be protected in a government-approved scheme within 30 days of receipt, and the prescribed information (the scheme, the dispute process, the landlord’s details and how the money can be reclaimed) must be served on the tenant inside the same 30 days. We use the DPS, and we do both.

We use the DPS, and we do both.

items.html: This protects you at least as much as the tenant. Under section 214 of the Housing Act 2004 a tenant can ask the county court to order a penalty of between one and three times the deposit if either duty is missed, and each renewal is treated as a separate tenancy, so a deposit that was never protected can generate that penalty several times over. At the end of the tenancy, disputes go to free adjudication decided purely on the evidence submitted. That is precisely why we photograph a proper inventory on the day the tenant moves in.

HMO · Licensing
Does my property need an HMO licence?

items.html: This is the question we are asked more than any other, and the honest answer is that it depends on two separate things: what the national rules say, and what your particular council has decided locally. Landlords get caught out by the second one.

items.html: First, is it an HMO at all?
items.text: First, is it an HMO at all?

items.html: A property is a House in Multiple Occupation when at least three tenants live there forming more than one household, and they share a kitchen, bathroom or toilet. “Household” means a family or a couple, so three friends renting a three-bedroom house together is an HMO, while a family of five is not. That definition catches a lot of ordinary shared houses in Fallowfield, Rusholme and Salford that landlords think of simply as a let.

items.html: Mandatory HMO licensing. Applies across England to any HMO occupied by five or more people forming two or more households. The old “three storeys or more” condition was removed in 2018, so a five-person HMO in a two-storey terrace needs a licence just as much as one in a large townhouse.

items.html: Additional licensing. A council can extend licensing to smaller HMOs, typically three or four occupants, in areas it designates. Manchester and Salford have both used these powers.

items.html: Operating an unlicensed property that requires a licence is a criminal offence. A council can issue a civil penalty of up to £30,000 per offence as an alternative to prosecution, and prosecution carries an unlimited fine. Separately, the tenants or the council can apply for a Rent Repayment Order requiring you to repay up to twelve months’ rent. On a room-let HMO at £450 a room that is a genuinely serious number.

items.html: A licence is not just a fee. Bringing a house up to that standard is usually where the real cost and the real delay sit, not the application form.

Compliance
Awaab's Law, damp and mould.

items.html: Damp and mould used to be treated as a maintenance annoyance and, too often, blamed on the tenant’s drying habits. That era is over. There are now fixed timescales attached to it, and the burden of proving you acted sits with the landlord.

Where the law came from

items.html: Awaab Ishak was a two-year-old boy in Rochdale who died in 2020 after prolonged exposure to mould in his family’s home. The rules that carry his name were introduced for social housing and have been extended to the private rented sector through the Renters’ Rights Act. The principle is simple: once a serious hazard is reported, the clock starts.

What it means in practice

items.html: You are required to investigate a reported damp or mould hazard within a set period, tell the tenant in writing what you found, and begin the remedial work within a further set period, with far shorter deadlines where the hazard poses a significant risk to health. The exact timescales are being phased in, and the sensible working assumption is days, not months.

items.html: Alongside this sits the Homes (Fitness for Human Habitation) Act, which already lets a tenant take a landlord to court directly over a property that is unfit, and the Housing Health and Safety Rating System, which councils use to assess hazards including damp, excess cold and fire risk.

The part landlords underestimate: evidence

items.html: Almost every dispute we have seen turns on records rather than facts. If a tenant reports mould and you send someone the same week, the difference between a resolved repair and a claim is whether you can show when it was reported, when you attended, what you found and what you did. A phone call that nobody wrote down is worth nothing eighteen months later.

What usually fixes it

items.html: Most of the damp we deal with in Manchester’s older housing stock is condensation rather than a leak or rising damp, and the fix is normally ventilation and heating rather than repainting. Extractor fans that actually run on a humidity sensor, trickle vents, insulation, and dealing with cold bridging solve far more cases than mould wash ever has. Where it is a genuine defect (a failed gutter, a slipped slate, a bridged damp course), painting over it simply restarts the clock.

The arithmetic

items.html: Take a property let at £1,000 a month. An empty month is not £1,000. It is the rent, plus council tax, which becomes your liability the moment the tenancy ends, plus standing charges on the utilities, plus the cost of re-letting, cleaning, any touch-up decorating, and the re-let fee. Realistically you are looking at £1,300 to £1,500 for that month.

items.html: It is the biggest change to private renting in thirty years, and most of it is already in force. This guide is for landlords who want to know what actually changed, what stayed the same, and what it means for how a tenancy runs day to day.

items.html: Assured shorthold tenancies have been replaced by assured periodic tenancies. Every tenancy now rolls month to month with no fixed end date, and a tenant can leave on two months’ notice. In practice that puts a premium on choosing the right tenant at the start, because the tenancy no longer locks anyone in for a year.
